4.text: I met several such wanderers. Some were still young, others were already

5.text: old; some had wives who wandered with them, others were all alone in the

6.text: world; some had at least a reindeer-team of their own, others had but a single

7.text: reindeer, and a few had none at all, though wandering in the tundra afoot

8.text: in the winter-time is quite difficult. There were men who had neither reindeer

9.text: nor rifle, nor even so much as a belt-knife, which to the arctic man is

10.text: almost as necessary as his right hand.

11.text: Wanderers are much neglected. Hunger is their constant companion.

12.text: I mentioned before that the Chukchee eat only once a day, and even the

13.text: coming of a guest of honor does not change this established rule. With the

14.text: “idle wanderer” it is still worse. In the evening, when meal-time at last

15.text: comes, he may, of course, according to custom, enter any house; but he will

16.text: be shown a place near the entrance, behind all other guests, and from this

17.text: place he is not able to reach the trough with his hands. The mistress of

18.text: the house will slip into his hand a few morsels of meat of the poorer quality,

19.text: and she will not expect him to ask for more. He will hardly be admitted

20.text: into the inner room to sleep; his sleeping-place is in the outer tent, under

21.text: some sledge, where the dogs sleep. The next day, if he stays in the camp,

22.text: he receives still less food, and is treated with less ceremony. Of course, if

23.text: he wants to take part in the daily work, — chop wood, carry water, catch

24.text: reindeer, etc., — his position may be changed; but then he ceases to be an

25.text: “idle wanderer.” Even old men thus inclined are harshly treated. One of

26.text: my acquaintances told me the following story: —

27.text: “Two years ago I was in the camp of G̣inuˊqäi. His older brother, Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê, carne

28.text: from Umekeˊt-wuiˊwun (‘Gathering Town,’ the name the Chukchee give to Nishne-Kolymsk, because

29.text: in the spring the trade-gatherings take place there). He came to his brother’s camp and staid

30.text: there a few days. Then they formed a corral of sledges to catch the driving-reindeer. At that

31.text: time there came many guests, — Vaaˊlɪrg̣ɪn, Ruˊltɪ, Êˊɪlhɪn, Rultuˊwg̣i with his wife. They drank

32.text: brandy. Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê began to abuse Rultuˊwg̣i, saying, ‘Why have you come hither? You

33.text: are a poor hungry man. You wander about in your hunger, seeking of food.’ Rultuˊwg̣i answered,

34.text: ‘There was a time when I assisted men in catching reindeer.’ — ‘Then why are you not doing

35.text: it now?’ Rultuˊwg̣i said, ‘I am now old. How shall I do it? In times past the old men sat

36.text: quietly, well treated by the host.’ — ‘No, no, you are the assisting one. Why are you sitting still?

37.text: Can you give assistance sitting thus?’ Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê said, ‘There, stop sitting, or I will strike

38.text: you on the head.’ Rultuˊwg̣i said, ‘Do it, if you have no shame. Do you wish to shamelessly

39.text: assault a man with an ailing back? My back causes me much suffering.’ Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê grew

40.text: angry, and said, ‘Well, well, let us have a match.’ Rultuˊwg̣i took off his belt, also his fur shirt.

41.text: Then he said, ‘All right! Have a wrestling-match with me.’ Both were tipsy. Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê

42.text: also took off his belt with the knife. He said, ‘No’ I will only strike you on your head.’ He

43.text: struck the old man with the belt upon the head. ‘Make yourself useful, quick, make yourself

44.text: useful!’, The old man cried, ‘Oh, oh, oh! Stop beating me! I will assist you.’ He put on his

45.text: shirt, took the lasso and the walking-staff, and ran to the reindeer. A little time after that,

46.text: Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê asked us, ‘Where is Rultuˊwg̣i?’ We said, ‘He has gone to herd.’ Tatk-Omruˊwg̣ê
